turns.text: real quick can u look up how long it takes to recover after a night shift and what to eat after. i work sun-thu nights 10pm-6:30am and sleep like 8am-1pm. is that even enough lol

Happy to help. Short version: a 5-hour sleep block is on the low side. Most adults need 7-9 hours in 24 hours, but that doesn't have to be one block. A nap before your shift can close the gap.

Recovery after a run of nights:
- One short night of sleep: usually back to normal within a day or two if you get a longer sleep after.
- A full stretch of night shifts: sleep debt can take several days of longer sleep to pay off.
- Your body clock adapts slowly, so keeping the same sleep time on days off helps.

What to eat after a shift:
- Go for protein plus some slow carbs, and keep it moderate so you can fall asleep. A huge meal can keep you awake.
- Avoid a lot of sugar and heavy greasy food right before bed.

eggs and rice usually. is that good. and yeah i got afternoon sections mon wed thu at 2 so i gotta be actually sharp by then not just awake

Eggs and rice is a solid recovery meal. Eggs give you protein, and rice gives you slow-ish carbs to refill energy. Add some fruit or veggies if you can, like spinach in the eggs or a banana on the side. Keep the portion moderate so it doesn't mess with sleep.

For being sharp by 2 p.m. on class days:
- Get light and some water within 30 minutes of waking. Sunlight is best, since it helps your brain switch on.
- Wake up at least an hour before class. Grogginess right after waking (sleep inertia) can last 30-60 minutes.
- Have a small meal or snack with protein after you get up.
- If you use caffeine, have it after you wake, not before bed.
- On days you have time, a 20-minute nap before your shift helps more than you'd think.

Good move using shared notes. To make them stick:
- Don't just reread. Turn each section into 2-3 questions and quiz yourself without looking.
- Write a short summary in your own words after each topic. That shows you what you actually understand.
- Compare the notes with the textbook or slides and mark any gaps. Ask your professor or a classmate about those.
- Do short sessions (25-30 minutes) with breaks. You'll retain more than with one long cram when you're tired.
- Study right after you wake up and eat, when you're sharpest, not right before your shift.
- Sketch diagrams or processes from memory, which works well for physiology.
